paragraph.text: the craving for meat exists, but it is largely learned and reinforced: by culture, by childhood, by salt, fat and seasoning. And even if it were entirely natural, a desire isn't a justification. We have many strong cravings that we don't follow when they would harm others.
"It's my body asking for it. The smell of a barbecue is irresistible for a reason."
Many people feel a strong, spontaneous craving to eat meat.
Strong, spontaneous cravings point to the body's needs.
Meeting the body's needs is legitimate.
P1 is true. The problem lies in P2, which treats desire as need, and in P3, which assumes that satisfying the body never conflicts with the interests of others.
"The smell of a barbecue is irresistible for a reason."
"I tried, but my body craves meat."
"If it weren't natural, why would it taste so good?"

Sometimes we really want to eat candy. That doesn't mean the body needs candy: it means candy tastes good and we're used to it. Meat is similar. And even when the craving is strong, we can think about whether it hurts someone before doing it.

Wanting isn't needing. Much of the taste for meat is learned from childhood and reinforced by salt, fat and seasoning, which also make well-seasoned plant versions very tasty. And even if the desire were natural, desires don't justify causing harm: we have many strong cravings we don't follow when they would hurt someone.
"Is there any other strong craving you don't follow because it would harm someone?"
That craving is a bodily need
False: well-planned vegan diets are adequate
So I may satisfy it even if someone else suffers
The body needs nutrients, not specific foods. Protein, iron and other nutrients can be obtained without meat, according to the US Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics.

text.bold: 2. Much of the taste is learned.

paragraph.text: Food preferences form through repeated exposure, especially in childhood, and change over time. Many people who stop eating meat report that the craving fades after a few weeks or months.

text.bold: 3. Much of the appeal is flavor, not the animal.

paragraph.text: The smell of a barbecue comes largely from charred fat, salt, smoke and seasoning. Plant products prepared the same way aren't identical, but they trigger many of the same responses, which shows that much of the desire is for flavors and textures that don't depend on anyone's death.
We have many strong cravings we don't follow when they would harm someone. That isn't denying nature; it's having ethics.
If the craving isn't a need, what's left is pleasure, and the eater's pleasure has to be weighed against what the animal loses.
Well-planned vegan diets are appropriate at all stages of life
Shows the craving doesn't correspond to a need
Repeated exposure, especially in childhood, shapes taste
; a review of repeated exposure and children's preferences
(d) The strongest counter-reply: cravings are hard to overcome

The most serious version doesn't say the craving justifies anything, but that it's real and strong, and that asking people to ignore it is asking too much. Ethics has to be realistic about what people can do.
(e) Why the counter-reply doesn't reach the conclusion

text.bold: It shifts to difficulty, not justification.

paragraph.text: Being hard doesn't make it right (E10).
With substitutes, seasoning and time, the craving tends to lose strength.

text.bold: Being realistic means helping people change, not excusing them from it.

paragraph.text: A realistic ethics offers paths, not excuses.

paragraph.text: What attracts is the flavor, not the origin.
The desire is promoted to a need because that excuses change
The principle being tested is: "if I feel a strong craving, satisfying it is legitimate".
Attacking whoever annoys us would be legitimate
Any desire would justify acting, even without consent
A craving to eat the neighbor's dog
It would be legitimate, if strong enough
The principle doesn't depend on species

The craving for meat is real, and it's dishonest to pretend otherwise. For many people, meat is tied to memories, affection and pleasure, and changing takes effort. Recognizing that matters for helping people through the transition.
But recognizing the strength of a craving isn't accepting it as a justification. Taste can change, flavors can be recreated, and the animal's life can't.
